# F · Needle and pointer readouts (F5–F15)

*Build-ready style entries for codes F5–F15, chosen from `p2-FG.md`. F1–F4
are in `p3-FG.md`; this file continues from F5 and uses the same format. One
priority-A entry per code (the definitive example), the rest B or C. Every
entry names the machine for reference only — builds use generic wordmarks and
never reproduce a logo or a maker's cartouche. Google-Font stand-ins are from
SPEC §3's list. Sizes are the natural size at `scale="1"` in CSS px and
include the bezel, case, window or panel scrap the element carries. Needles
have ballistics (SPEC §3); every entry says which. Slugs were checked against
every `p3-*.md` — `meter-turn-slip-ball` (F4.3) already covers the aircraft
slip ball, and the A16 bezels already cover the Navitimer and dive bezels, so
F7, F10 and F12 below deliberately choose around them.*

---

## F5 · Gauge, Bourdon-tube style

### F5.1 · Ashcroft-pattern brass boiler gauge — white enamel dial, Didone figures, red line
- slug: `gauge-ashcroft-steam-brass`
- element: `sk-gauge-ashcroft-steam`
- kind: output
- value: range 0–300 step 1 unit psi (`max` configurable 160 / 300 / 400; `redline` attribute draws the hand-painted working-pressure line, default 200)
- machine: Ashcroft Mfg. Co. 6-inch and 8½-inch locomotive and stationary boiler gauges, Bridgeport CT, 1880s–1920s (Crosby and Dewrance made the same object)
- era: 1900s
- origin: USA
- size: 6-inch case with a 5-inch dial → build at 200 × 200 px (dial 160 px inside a 20 px brass ring)
- materials: cast brass case with a screwed-on brass bezel ring, polished but dulled, with two small fine-slot screws at 12 and 6 in the bezel; thick bevelled glass with a bright crescent glint on the bevel; white porcelain-enamel dial with a hairline crazing pattern; engraved black Didone numerals; a slim blued-steel spade pointer with a brass counterweight tail; a brass pivot boss at centre; a ¼-inch brass pipe stub leaving the case at 6 o'clock
- palette: brass #c9a24c highlight #f0dc95 shadow #6e5220, patina spots #7f6a3c at 20 %, enamel #f5f1e6 with crazing lines #d9d2c2 at 40 %, numerals #1c1a17, red line #b8231a, pointer blued #23304a with a highlight #6a7a99, glass bevel glint #ffffff at 70 %
- typeface: engraved Didone / Scotch Roman figures → no Didone on the list; use Google "Libre Franklin" 700 at ~11 px for the numerals with the thin strokes drawn as SVG-path serifs on 0, 1 and 4 where cheap, and "Libre Franklin" 600 caps 6 px tracking 0.25em for "POUNDS" and "STEAM"
- the tells:
  1. the numerals sit in a *full* 270° circle with 0 at about 7 o'clock and the top of the range at about 5 o'clock; each numeral is upright-to-the-radius (rotated), not upright-to-the-page
  2. the red line is hand-painted: a slightly wavy 2 px radial stroke between the arc and the numeral ring, fatter at the inner end, with a tiny bleed
  3. a generic maker's cartouche in the centre — an oval of fine engraved rules with "STEAM GAUGE" in caps and a city line below, never a real eagle or name
  4. the pointer is a slim spade: a fine shaft that widens to a leaf 4 mm before the tip and narrows again; the tail is short and ends in a round brass counterweight
  5. brass bezel ring with a knurled outer edge (fine radial hatching) and a flat polished face carrying the two screws, plus a soft warm reflection of the light on the ring's upper left
  6. the enamel is not perfectly white: a faint warm vignette toward the edges and two or three brown "flea-bite" chips at the rim, one under the bezel screw at 6
  7. minor ticks every 2 psi, major every 10, with the 50s slightly longer; the arc line is thick (1.5 px) and black
- motion: heavy Bourdon ballistics — 450 ms ease-out with a 5 % overshoot and a second smaller bounce; a slight needle tremor (0.3° at 6 Hz, decaying) when the value settles, as if steam were pulsing
- states to show: 155 psi with the red line at 200; 0 (pointer resting on a small brass stop pin at 7 o'clock); one at scale 0.6 in a pair
- priority: A

### F5.2 · US fleet-boat submarine depth gauge — white on black, red test-depth arc
- slug: `gauge-depth-fleet-boat`
- element: `sk-gauge-depth-fleet-boat`
- kind: output
- value: range 0–450 step 1 unit ft (`max` 450 or 600; `testdepth` attribute sets where the red arc begins, default 300)
- machine: US Navy Gato/Balao-class control-room depth gauge, US Gauge Co. / Kollsman, 1941–1945
- era: 1940s
- origin: USA
- size: 8-inch gauge → build at 220 × 220 px
- materials: black-enamelled steel case with a thin polished brass bezel that has been painted over black on the flat face and worn back to brass on the rim; flat glass; matte black dial; white painted numerals and ticks; a fat white pointer with a black centre line and a white-outlined black tail; a black domed pivot cap; a small red arc painted between the ticks and the numerals at the deep end
- palette: dial #0b0c0d, markings #ecece4, red arc #c0201c, pointer white #f2f2ee with a shadow #000 at 40 % offset 1 px, bezel black #17181a with worn brass rim #a88a45, case #1e1f21, glass glint #ffffff at 5 % as a soft diagonal band
- typeface: US Navy instrument grotesque → Google "Barlow" 600 at 12 px for the numerals, "Barlow" 500 caps 7 px tracking 0.2em for "FEET" and "DEPTH"
- the tells:
  1. white-on-black in a 300° sweep — the 0 at 7 o'clock and 450 at 5 o'clock, big open numerals every 50 with fat white ticks every 10 and hairline ticks every 2
  2. the red arc at the deep end hugs the outside of the tick ring from `testdepth` to max; it is painted a little unevenly, wider at its start
  3. the pointer is *fat*: a 5 px white blade with a fine black centre line running its length, and a stubby tail outlined in white on black
  4. "FEET" in small caps under the pivot, "DEPTH" above it; nothing else on the dial
  5. a faint ring of grey where the bezel has been repainted, and two bare-brass wear crescents on the rim at 3 and 9 where hands grip it
  6. optional `secondary` boolean draws a tiny 0–165 ft "shallow" companion gauge to the right at 40 % scale, sharing the value
- motion: fluid-damped — 700 ms critically damped approach with no overshoot, then a slow 0.5° wander (0.1 Hz) when idle to suggest the boat trimming
- states to show: 220 ft; 315 ft (pointer inside the red arc); one at scale 0.7 beside the shallow companion
- priority: B

### F5.3 · Welding-regulator cylinder gauge — "USE NO OIL" in red across the face
- slug: `gauge-regulator-use-no-oil`
- element: `sk-gauge-regulator-oxy`
- kind: output
- value: range 0–4000 step 10 unit psi (`gas` attribute "oxygen" | "acetylene" swaps the scale to 0–400 and the red band position; `overpressure` sets the red band start)
- machine: Victor / Harris two-gauge oxy-acetylene regulator gauges, 2-inch steel case, 1930s–present
- era: 1950s
- origin: USA
- size: 2-inch gauge → build at 120 × 120 px, plus a 24 px brass stem at 6 o'clock
- materials: pressed-steel case in dull chrome with a rolled front lip; a plastic (or thin glass) crystal that is faintly scratched; white paper dial with black numerals; a short black needle with a brass hub; a red "OVERPRESSURE" band at the top of the range; "USE NO OIL" printed in red in an arc across the upper face; a brass ⅛-inch NPT stem at the bottom with two hex flats
- palette: case chrome #d8d8d4 highlight #ffffff shadow #6f7070, dial #f7f5ee, numerals #1a1917, red text and band #cc2a1f, needle #111, hub brass #b99a4c, stem brass #a6853c with hex-flat facets #c8a95a / #7b6128, crystal scratches #ffffff at 25 %
- typeface: cheap offset-printed industrial grotesque → Google "Roboto Condensed" 700 at 9 px numerals; "Roboto Condensed" 700 caps 7 px for "USE NO OIL"; "Roboto Condensed" 400 5 px for "PSI" and "kPa"
- the tells:
  1. "USE NO OIL" in red caps in an arc across the top of the dial, between the arc and the pivot — the one thing everyone remembers
  2. a 270° scale with the numerals *inside* the tick ring and a second, smaller kPa scale in red just inside them (dual scale, both crowded)
  3. a short stubby black needle — barely reaching the ticks — on a tiny brass hub with a slot
  4. the chrome case's rolled front lip is a thin bright ring with a dark inner shadow onto the crystal; the crystal has two fine arc scratches and a fingerprint smudge
  5. the brass stem with its two hex flats leaves the case at 6 o'clock and has a thread-tape whisker of white at the joint
  6. a small red overpressure band at the top of the range with a diagonal hatch in it
  7. on `gas="acetylene"` the numerals are 0–400 and a second red "DO NOT EXCEED 15 PSI" arc appears on the low-pressure gauge — skip on the high-pressure one
- motion: quick and slightly sticky — 300 ms ease-out, then the needle catches for 100 ms at ~90 % and finishes in a small step (Bourdon-tube friction)
- states to show: oxygen 1850 psi; acetylene 250 psi; one pair at scale 0.8 side by side as they sit on a regulator
- priority: B

### F5.4 · Aneroid barometer with the manual brass set-hand — the word scale
- slug: `barometer-aneroid-stormoguide`
- element: `sk-barometer-aneroid`
- kind: both (the black pointer is output; the brass set-hand is an input, dragged around the glass)
- value: range 28.0–31.0 step 0.01 unit inHg (also renders mb 950–1050 inside); `set` attribute holds the brass hand's position and dispatches `change` when dragged
- machine: Short & Mason "Stormoguide" / Negretti & Zambra domestic aneroid, brass-cased, 1900s–1950s
- era: 1920s
- origin: UK
- size: 6-inch brass case → build at 220 × 220 px
- materials: a turned brass bezel with a rolled edge; bevelled glass with a small brass knob at its centre that turns the set-hand; a silvered (matte, faintly grainy) brass dial with engraved lettering filled black; a blued-steel main pointer; a slim brass set-hand with a wire tip; the case sits on a walnut backboard scrap
- palette: brass #c8a656 highlight #f2e3ad shadow #6d5320, silvered dial #e6e3d8 with a grain texture #d7d3c6 at 30 %, engraving #1f1d19, blued pointer #2b3650, set-hand brass #d1b262, walnut #5a3a22 → #7a4f2e, glass edge #ffffff at 55 %
- typeface: Victorian engraved capitals for the word scale → Google "Libre Franklin" 600 caps 8 px tracking 0.3em; numerals "Libre Franklin" 500 at 9 px; "STORMY RAIN CHANGE FAIR VERY DRY" in a single arc
- the tells:
  1. the word scale on the upper arc — "STORMY · RAIN · CHANGE · FAIR · VERY DRY" — with CHANGE dead centre at 12 and small engraved rules between the words
  2. two hands from the same centre: a blued-steel pointer and a slimmer *brass* set-hand with a wire tip that the person leaves where the reading was yesterday
  3. the small knurled brass knob at the centre of the glass, with a glint, which drags the set-hand (input); the main pointer never responds to the pointer
  4. the silvered dial's fine grain and a slightly darker ring where the glass rim shades it
  5. a millibar scale inside the inch scale in smaller engraved figures, and "RISE" / "FALL" curved beside the pivot
  6. the brass bezel is turned, with three fine concentric grooves on its face catching the light
  7. the walnut backboard shows below the case with a keyhole hanger at the top
- motion: extremely slow — the main pointer approaches over 2 s with no overshoot; the set-hand follows the drag directly and stays where released
- states to show: 29.60 with the set-hand at 30.10 ("falling"); 30.30 with the set-hand under the pointer; one at scale 0.65
- priority: C

## F6 · Automotive gauge

### F6.1 · Smiths black-dial tachometer with chrome bezel (Jaguar E-Type / Mk2 cluster)
- slug: `gauge-smiths-etype-tach`
- element: `sk-gauge-smiths-tach`
- kind: output
- value: range 0–6000 step 10 unit rpm (`role` attribute "tach" | "speedo" swaps to 0–160 mph with the odometer; `redline` default 5500)
- machine: Smiths Industries tachometer (RV series) and speedometer (SN series) as fitted to the Jaguar E-Type Series 1 and Mk2, 1961–1968
- era: 1960s
- origin: UK
- size: 5-inch instrument → build at 200 × 200 px (a 4-inch version for the small gauges at scale 0.55)
- materials: a flat matte black dial; white printed numerals and ticks; a bright chrome bezel with a rolled outer edge and a flat inner face; a slightly domed glass; a white needle from a black domed centre boss with a chrome ring; a small square window at 6 o'clock with a five-drum odometer on the speedo, or a small clock inset on the tach (E-Type)
- palette: dial #0f0f10, markings #efece3, red arc #c9271f, bezel chrome #e9e9e6 → #8a8c8d → #3a3b3c, needle #f4f2ea with a black shadow at 35 %, boss #131313 with a chrome ring #d5d5d2, odometer drums #f1eee6 on #1a1a1a, glass dome glint #ffffff at 8 % as a soft ellipse in the upper left
- typeface: Smiths' narrow Gill-like grotesque → Google "Barlow Condensed" 500 at 13 px numerals; "Barlow Condensed" 500 caps 7 px tracking 0.15em for "RPM ×100" and "MPH"; no maker wordmark — "MADE IN ENGLAND" in 5 px caps under the boss instead
- the tells:
  1. numerals 0–60 (×100) around a 270° sweep starting at ~7 o'clock; every numeral is *upright to the page*, not rotated, and slightly condensed
  2. the red arc is painted *inside* the tick ring from 5500 to 6000 and is thin (2 px) — on this dial the red is a line, not a wedge
  3. the chrome bezel is the fattest thing on the gauge: 12 px wide, with a bright top-left highlight, a dark lower-right, and a thin black rubber seal visible between it and the glass
  4. the needle is a white blade with a subtle taper, rising from a large black boss that has a chrome ring around it and a slight dome highlight
  5. a small rectangular window at 6 o'clock: on the speedo the odometer's five drums (last one red on the trip); on the tach an inset clock face with two tiny hands (drawn static)
  6. "RPM ×100" in two lines above the boss and "MADE IN ENGLAND" below it in tiny caps
  7. the dial's black is not flat: a very faint radial gradient lighter near the centre from the domed glass, and the glass's elliptical glint
- motion: classic magnetic-drag speedo lag — 400 ms ease-out with a 2 % overshoot, plus a 0.5° flutter at idle values below 1000 rpm
- states to show: 3200 rpm; 5800 rpm (in the red); speedo mode at 72 mph with the odometer reading 41,377
- priority: A

### F6.2 · 1959 Cadillac red-ribbon speedometer — the growing red band in a chrome window
- slug: `speedo-cadillac-ribbon-1959`
- element: `sk-speedo-ribbon-cadillac`
- kind: output
- value: range 0–120 step 1 unit mph
- machine: GM (AC Spark Plug division) ribbon speedometer in the 1959–60 Cadillac and 1958–60 Impala dashes
- era: 1950s
- origin: USA
- size: a wide horizontal window ~14 × 3 inches → build at 420 × 110 px including the chrome surround
- materials: a horizontal chrome-plated die-cast bezel with a slight top-to-bottom curve and rounded ends; a smoked, slightly convex plastic lens; behind it a white or silver-grey scale strip with gold-anodised numerals 0–120 and short black ticks; the indicator is a **red ribbon** (a rotating drum painted half red, half black, seen edge-on through the slot) that grows from the left as speed rises; a small "GEN" and "OIL" jewel at each end of the bezel
- palette: bezel chrome #efefec → #9c9d9e → #4a4b4d, scale strip #e8e6df, numerals gold #c9a63b with a darker #8c6f22 edge, ticks #1b1b1b, ribbon red #d62a1f with a top highlight #f26a5c and a lower shade #8f1a12, ribbon's black remainder #121213, lens tint #000 at 15 %, jewels #d0241b / #d18a1a
- typeface: the gold GM numerals are a wide 50s grotesque → Google "Libre Franklin" 700 at 14 px, letter-spaced 0.05em; "MPH" in "Libre Franklin" 600 caps 7 px
- the tells:
  1. the reading is a *band*, not a needle: a red bar that lengthens from the left edge across the numerals, with a soft rolling highlight along its top edge because the drum is cylindrical
  2. the leading end of the ribbon is a *vertical* edge (the drum's painted boundary), never a tapered pointer
  3. the numerals sit above the slot in gold on a pale strip, evenly spaced (the scale is linear), with a slightly heavier 0 and 120 at the ends
  4. the chrome bezel is a wide, gently curved band with a bright reflection running its whole length and a shadow underneath onto the dash
  5. the convex lens adds a faint horizontal glint across the upper third and darkens the slot's edges
  6. two tiny jewel lamps set into the bezel ends (generator, oil), unlit by default; `warn` attribute lights them
  7. a scrap of the dash's ribbed brushed aluminium behind the bezel, with a grain that runs horizontally
- motion: the drum has inertia — 500 ms ease-out with no overshoot but a visible slow creep of the last 2 mph; at speed the ribbon's highlight shimmers slightly as the drum turns
- states to show: 35 mph; 88 mph; one at scale 0.6 with `warn` on
- priority: B

### F6.3 · Porsche 911 VDO tachometer — green night glow, red zone, big centre dial
- slug: `tach-vdo-911-green`
- element: `sk-tach-vdo-911`
- kind: output
- value: range 0–8000 step 10 unit rpm (`redline` default 6800; `lit` boolean turns on the green night illumination)
- machine: VDO tachometer, centre dial of the Porsche 911 five-gauge fan, 1969–1989 (the 1970s green-numeral cars)
- era: 1970s
- origin: West Germany
- size: 100 mm instrument → build at 200 × 200 px
- materials: a matte black dial with a slight satin sheen; numerals and ticks printed in a pale green-white that glows green when lit; a thin black bezel with a fine chrome inner ring; flat glass; a white needle with an orange-red tip on late cars, white on early — use white; a small black boss; a red zone as a painted wedge; a tiny round warning lamp cluster in the lower half (oil, alternator) on the real dial — draw two unlit red lamps
- palette: dial #111212, markings unlit #cfe0c6, markings lit #8cff8a with a glow #3aff6a at 35 % (blur 3 px), red zone #c8241c (lit #ff3a30), bezel #0a0a0a with a chrome ring #b9bcbd, needle #f2f1eb, boss #0e0e0e, lamps #6c1a15 unlit / #ff3b2f lit
- typeface: VDO's DIN 1451 → Google "Oswald" 400 at 14 px numerals (Oswald is the DIN stand-in per SPEC), "Oswald" 400 caps 7 px tracking 0.1em for "1/min" and "×100"
- the tells:
  1. a big 300° sweep with 0 at about 7 o'clock and 8 (thousand) at about 5 o'clock; numerals every 1000 in a DIN face, every one upright to the page
  2. the red zone is a solid wedge painted between the outer tick ring and the numerals from 6800 to 8000, not just a line
  3. `lit`: everything printed glows green — the numerals, the ticks and the needle's base — with a soft bloom, and the dial stays black; the red zone glows red
  4. the bezel is *thin* and black with a hairline chrome ring just inside it — the opposite of the Smiths' fat chrome
  5. the needle is a plain white blade, slightly wider at the boss, with no counterweight visible; the boss is small and black
  6. "1/min" and "×100" in small DIN caps below the centre, and a small VDO-style diamond-shaped index mark (generic) at 12
  7. two tiny round lamps at 5 and 7 o'clock inside the dial, dark red when off
- motion: eager sports-car needle — 250 ms ease-out with a 3 % overshoot; a small 1° twitch at every value change above 6000
- states to show: 3400 rpm unlit; 7100 rpm lit (in the red, everything glowing); one at scale 0.75 lit
- priority: B

### F6.4 · Citroën CX drum speedometer — a rotating cylinder under a curved lens
- slug: `speedo-citroen-cx-drum`
- element: `sk-speedo-cx-drum`
- kind: output
- value: range 0–220 step 1 unit km/h
- machine: Jaeger drum speedometer in the Citroën CX "lunule" dashboard, 1974–1985

- origin: France

- typeface: Jaeger's 70s grotesque → Google "Roboto Condensed" 700 at 16 px numerals; "Roboto Condensed" 400 7 px for "km/h"
- the tells:
  1. the reading is under a **fixed red line** at the window's centre, and the numbers slide *behind* it — the value increases by the drum turning, so 80 slides right-to-left past the line
  2. the numerals crowd and foreshorten toward both sides of the window (cylindrical projection) and darken into the drum's shadow at the edges
  3. the magnifying lens: a horizontal glint band across the upper part, and the numerals nearest the centre are drawn 10 % larger than those at the edges (lens magnification stacked on the projection)
  4. ticks every 5 km/h as short black lines on the drum, every 20 with a numeral
  5. a fine horizontal seam where the drum's printed band meets the hood, and a soft hood shadow across the top of the drum
  6. the odometer below: five white-on-black drums and a three-drum trip with a red last drum
- motion: the drum has real inertia — 600 ms ease-in-out with no overshoot, and while moving the numerals blur very slightly (opacity 80 % on the moving numerals during the tween)
- states to show: 50 km/h; 130 km/h; one at scale 0.7
- priority: C

  7. tiny legend lines: "ALT" under the 12, "1000 FEET" and "100 FEET" beside small hand icons, "CALIBRATED TO 20,000 FEET" in an arc above the 6

## F8 · Compass / gyro / heading card

### F8.1 · Aircraft "whiskey" compass — the vertical drum card in a window
- slug: `compass-airpath-whiskey-drum`
- element: `sk-compass-whiskey-drum`
- kind: output
- value: angle 0–360 step 1 unit degrees (`card` attribute "latin" | "cyrillic" swaps N E S W for С В Ю З)
- machine: Airpath C2300 / Kollsman B-16 magnetic compass in the windscreen post of light aircraft, 1940s–present
- era: 1950s
- origin: USA
- size: 60 × 60 mm body with a 40 × 22 mm window → build at 130 × 150 px including the mounting bracket and the correction card beneath
- materials: a small black-painted aluminium cylinder lying on its side, with a rounded front and a rectangular glass window; inside, a fluid-filled bowl with a **vertical drum card** — white marks on black — reading "N 3 6 E 12 15 S 21 24 W 30 33"; a fixed white lubber line down the centre of the window; two small brass compensator screws on the top face marked N-S and E-W; a small white correction card in a bent-metal frame below the body with a hand-lettered table; a tiny bubble at the top of the fluid
- palette: body #1b1c1e with a #3a3b3e edge highlight, card drum #0b0c0d, marks #ebe8db, lubber line #f4f2ea, fluid tint #08090b with a #ffffff at 6 % glint at the window's top edge, bubble #cfd3d6 at 60 %, compensator screws brass #b69645, correction card #f3f0e6 with #2a2a2a pencil-grey lettering and a red "FOR" heading #b7241c
- typeface: Google "Barlow" 600 at 10 px for the card figures and letters; the correction card in "Special Elite" 7 px (typewritten table "FOR 0 30 60 … STEER …")
- the tells:
  1. the card is a *drum*: the figures curve away at both edges of the window (cylindrical projection, crowding toward the sides), and the figure under the lubber line is the reading
  2. it reads *backwards* to a map — E is to the *left* of N on the drum as seen through the window, because you are looking at the far side of the card; builders must get this right
  3. every 30° a figure (dropping the trailing zero: 3, 6, 12…), every 10° a long tick, every 5° a short tick; N E S W replace 0, 9, 18, 27
  4. the window is small and the body large: a fat black cylinder with a rounded front, a bevelled window frame, and the two brass compensator screws on top
  5. a small bubble in the fluid at the top of the window, and a faint glint on the fluid's surface
  6. the correction card beneath, typewritten, in a bent tin frame with two screws
  7. the card overswings: in motion it leads then settles (the classic compass lag/lead)
- motion: liquid-damped with overshoot — 700 ms ease-out with an 8° overshoot and two decaying swings; a slow 1° sway when idle
- states to show: 045; 270 (W under the line); `card="cyrillic"` at 180 at scale 0.8
- priority: A

## F9 · Tuning eye / magic eye tube

### F9.1 · RCA 6E5 round "cat's eye" — the closing wedge shadow
- slug: `magic-eye-rca-6e5`
- element: `sk-magic-eye-6e5`
- kind: output
- value: range 0–100 (signal; 0 = shadow fully open ~90°, 100 = closed; `overlap` boolean lets the edges cross above 100 for the 6U5 look)
- machine: RCA 6E5 / 6U5 tuning-eye tube end-viewed through a dial escutcheon, Zenith and RCA console radios, 1935–1950s
- era: 1930s
- origin: USA
- size: ~1-inch phosphor target in a 1½-inch escutcheon hole → build at 96 × 96 px
- materials: a round hole in a chrome or brass escutcheon ring set into a walnut-veneer scrap; inside, the glass end of a tube with a green-glowing willemite phosphor ring; a dark centre cap (the cathode shield) with a tiny hot spot; a pie-shaped dark shadow that shrinks as the signal rises; the glass adds a faint dome reflection
- palette: phosphor #7bffa0 with a hotter inner edge #b6ffcb and a darker outer #3fbf68, shadow #0b1a10, centre cap #14181a with a #ff9b4a filament glint at 40 %, escutcheon chrome #dedfdb → #7d7f80, walnut #4a2f1c → #6b4528, glass dome glint #ffffff at 10 %
- typeface: none on the eye; a "TUNING" legend beneath in Google "Josefin Sans" 400 caps 6 px tracking 0.3em (the 30s Futura look)
- the tells:
  1. a green *ring* of light, not a disc — the centre is a dark cap, and the light is an annulus between the cap and the outer glass
  2. the shadow is a *wedge* opening from the centre toward 6 o'clock: wide (~90°) at no signal, narrowing to a hairline at full signal; its edges are soft (2 px feather) and slightly brighter just outside the shadow
  3. the phosphor has grain: a fine noise texture at 8 % opacity, and the glow blooms 3 px beyond the ring's edge onto the escutcheon
  4. the cathode shield cap at centre is matte black with a faint orange filament glint on its lower edge
  5. the escutcheon: a narrow chrome ring with a bright top-left highlight set into walnut veneer, with a dark inner shadow onto the glass
  6. with `overlap`, the two edges of the wedge cross at strong signal, producing a slightly brighter overlap sliver (the 6U5 "overlapping" eye)
  7. the glow has a very slow breathing (±3 % over 4 s) even at a fixed value — it is a hot tube
- motion: fast and electronic — 120 ms ease-out with no overshoot; add the breathing and a 1-frame flicker on large jumps
- states to show: 15 (wide open); 85 (nearly closed); `overlap` at 110 at scale 1.3 to show the crossing
- priority: A

### F9.2 · EM84 bar eye — two green bars growing toward the centre
- slug: `magic-eye-em84-bar`
- element: `sk-magic-eye-em84`
- kind: output
- value: range 0–100 (0 = bars at the ends only, 100 = bars meeting; `overlap` boolean lets them cross for the overload look)
- machine: Philips / Mullard / Telefunken EM84 side-viewed indicator as a record-level meter on Grundig TK and Telefunken tape recorders and 1960s German radios, 1959–1970s
- era: 1960s
- origin: West Germany / Netherlands
- size: a 40 × 8 mm slot in the panel → build at 140 × 36 px including the surround
- materials: a horizontal rectangular slot in a brushed-aluminium or cream-painted panel scrap with a slightly rounded window; behind it the tube's flat green phosphor strip, dark grey when unlit; two bright green bars grow inward from each end; the gap between them is the dark unexcited phosphor; a fine glass reflection across the top; a tiny "▼" overload mark printed at the centre of the surround
- palette: phosphor lit #7bffa0 with a hot core #c8ffd8, unlit strip #16261b, overlap zone #dfffe8, panel aluminium #cfd1cd with a #ffffff grain at 20 %, or cream #e9e4d6, window shadow #000 at 50 % inner, mark #1a1a1a
- typeface: Google "Oswald" 400 caps 6 px for "AUSSTEUERUNG" / "LEVEL" above the slot (DIN-like, German gear)
- the tells:
  1. the bars grow *inward from both ends* toward the centre, symmetric, and the reading is the *gap* between them closing
  2. the bars' leading edges are soft and the bar itself has a brighter core line along its length (the phosphor is brightest where the electron beam is densest)
  3. at `overlap` the bars cross and the overlap sliver glows brighter — the "Übersteuerung" that tape-recorder owners learned to avoid
  4. the unlit strip is not black but dark green-grey, and the whole strip glows faintly even at 0
  5. the window is a narrow slot with a dark inner shadow on its upper edge and a hairline highlight on its lower edge, set in brushed aluminium with horizontal grain
  6. a small triangle index printed on the panel at the slot's centre
- motion: fast attack (60 ms), slower release (300 ms) — it is a level meter; add a ±2 % shimmer at 25 Hz on the bar edges
- states to show: 30; 95 (nearly meeting); `overlap` at 115; cream panel variant at scale 1.2
- priority: B

- the tells:
  1. the vial is barrel-curved: the bubble is bigger and brighter at the centre of its travel and squashes as it nears the ends; it is *above* the fluid's centre line, hugging the glass top
  2. the two black lines are etched *around* the glass and read as short vertical ellipses with the fluid refracting them slightly thicker where they cross the bubble
  3. the bubble is a bright ellipse with a crescent highlight top-left and a dark green edge, and it casts a faint shadow onto the fluid below
  4. the brass port's opening has a bevel with a bright top edge and a dark lower edge, two screw slots at random angles, and a thin line of grime in the joint
  5. the rosewood grain runs lengthwise with a brass binding strip along the edge
  6. `value` outside ±1 pins the bubble against the vial's end, squashed flat
- motion: fluid — 600 ms ease-out with a 10 % overshoot and a wobble (the bubble is light and the fluid viscous), plus a small settle tremor
- states to show: 0 (dead level); +0.4 (bubble touching the right line); −0.9 in aluminium at scale 0.8
- priority: A

- slug: `level-bullseye-tripod`

- origin: Japan

- materials: a black anodised or plastic ring with a rolled edge; a domed clear acrylic vial with green-yellow fluid and two (or three) concentric black rings etched on the inside of the dome; a round bubble that slides to the high side; a small drop shadow onto the panel it is let into
- palette: ring #171718 with a #3c3c3e highlight, fluid #b8d64a → #7f9f2c at the rim, rings #111, bubble #f3f7e8 with #ffffff highlight and a #6f8f22 edge, dome glint #ffffff at 35 % as an off-centre ellipse
- typeface: none
- the tells:
  1. the bubble is round and moves in two axes; it is largest at the centre and shrinks and distorts against the dome as it nears the rim
  2. two concentric etched circles, the inner one the "level" target; the bubble sits *inside* the inner circle when level
  3. the dome: a bright off-centre glint ellipse near the top-left, and a darker gradient toward the rim where the fluid deepens
  4. the black ring is thin with a rolled outer edge and a dark inner shadow onto the fluid
  5. the bubble casts a soft shadow onto the vial floor offset toward the low side

- origin: USA

- materials: a fan-shaped (~170°) white porcelain-enamel dial with black slab-serif numerals and ounce ticks; a cast-iron frame enamelled in cream with an ornamental lip and a chrome-plated bezel; a long, tapered black pointer with a small counterweight; a horizontal slogan arc "NO SPRINGS" / "HONEST WEIGHT" (generic — the phrase is fine, no logo); a brass or nickel pan hinted below the frame
- palette: enamel #f6f3ea with a #e5e0d4 rim shading and a #c9c3b3 crazing at 20 %, numerals #17150f, red #b9231a for the "lb" markers at each whole pound, frame cream #ece3cc with a #b9ab8c shadow and chips to #4a4238 iron, chrome bezel #e4e4e1 → #8b8d8e, pointer #101010, brass pan #c9a24c
- typeface: slab-serif enamel figures → none on the list; use Google "Courier Prime" 700 at 13 px (its slab serifs read right) for the numerals and "Bebas Neue" 10 px tracking 0.2em for the slogan
- the tells:
  1. the dial is a *fan* — a 170° sector standing on a squat iron base, with the pivot at the bottom centre; not a full circle
  2. pounds every 1 with sixteen ounce ticks between (¼-lb ticks longer), figures large, black and slab-seriffed on porcelain
  3. the pointer is a long black blade from the pivot to the tick ring with a fine tip and a small round counterweight tail below the pivot
  4. the porcelain's crazing and the frame's chipped enamel at the corners showing dark iron beneath
  5. the slogan in an arc above the pivot in caps, and a small "CAPACITY 30 LB" line beneath
  6. the chrome bezel is a narrow, bright ring around the fan's arc, following it and returning down the sides
  7. the pointer swings *past* the value and back — it is a pendulum-and-cam mechanism ("no springs")
- motion: pendulum ballistics — 900 ms with three decaying swings of 6°, 2°, 0.5° (the store scale settling); no tremor at rest
- states to show: 2 lb 6 oz; 14.75 lb; one at scale 0.55

### F12.1 · Swiss railway station clock — red ball second hand, stop-to-go
- slug: `clock-sbb-mobatime-stop-to-go`
- element: `sk-clock-station-stop-to-go`
- kind: output
- value: time (`value` accepts "HH:MM:SS" or a Unix ms number; default follows the live clock; `run` boolean, default true)
- machine: Hans Hilfiker's 1944 Swiss Federal Railways station clock as made by Mobatime / Moser-Baer, 1944–present
- era: 1940s
- origin: Switzerland
- size: a 400 mm platform clock → build at 200 × 200 px
- materials: a pure white matte dial in a black-painted steel ring; black rectangular bar indices (long at the hours, short at the minutes — no numerals); black baton hour and minute hands with squared ends; a red second hand with a round red disc ("ball") near its tip; flat glass with a soft reflection; a slim black rim
- palette: dial #f7f7f4, indices and hands #111214, second hand #d5281c with the ball #d5281c and a #ff5a4e highlight dot, rim #17181a, glass #ffffff at 6 % as a diagonal band, shadow under the hands #000 at 20 %
- typeface: none — the dial has no figures
- the tells:
  1. no numerals: sixty minute bars and twelve fatter hour bars, all rectangular, black on white, ending at a clean ring
  2. the hands are batons with square ends and the minute hand reaches exactly to the inner end of the minute bars
  3. the red second hand with its disc near the tip — the disc's diameter is about the width of two minute bars
  4. **stop-to-go**: the second hand sweeps the full circle in 58.5 s, stops dead at 12, waits ~1.5 s, then the minute hand *jumps* one bar and the second hand sets off again
  5. the minute hand moves only in one-minute jumps (with a small 0.3° overshoot bounce) — never smoothly
  6. the black rim is thin and matte with a hairline highlight; the dial is dead flat
- motion: as tell 4 and 5 — the sweep is continuous (rAF), the pause at 12 is exact, the minute jump has a 120 ms bounce; `run="false"` freezes everything at `value`
- states to show: live time running; 10:09:30 frozen; one at scale 0.6
- priority: A

- palette: panel #6f7b6e wrinkle with a #8a968a highlight and #4e574d pits, meter flange #1a1815 with a #3b3630 edge, card #f1ede0, black scale #1b1a17, red scale #c1272d, pointer #111, glass glint #ffffff at 7 %
- typeface: Google "Libre Franklin" 600 at 9 px for the S figures; "Libre Franklin" 600 7 px red for "+20 +40 +60"; "Libre Franklin" 500 caps 5 px tracking 0.2em for "S-UNITS" and "DB OVER S9"
- the tells:
  1. the scale changes colour at S9 — black to the left, red to the right — with a fat red tick at the 9
  2. the S figures are odd only (1 3 5 7 9), evenly spaced; the dB figures are +20 +40 +60, compressed
  3. a 90° arc on a square face with the pivot low and a small black boss; the pointer is a black knife edge with a tiny counterweight cross
  4. the meter flange is square, black, with rounded corners and four fine screw heads; the glass is slightly domed with a low glint
  5. the panel: grey-green wrinkle texture (a fine random cell pattern at 20 % contrast) with two chrome hex screws at the meter's corners
  6. "S-UNITS" under the arc and "DB OVER S9" under the red half, both tiny
- motion: an S-meter is fast — 150 ms rise, 400 ms fall (AGC), with a 2 Hz ±1 % breathing at rest (band noise)
- states to show: S7; S9+30; one at scale 0.8
- priority: A

### F14.2 · 1970s Japanese transceiver multi-scale meter — cool-lit face, stacked ALC / IP / RF scales
- slug: `smeter-kenwood-ts520-multiscale`
- element: `sk-smeter-multiscale`
- kind: output
- value: range 0–100 (`scale` attribute "s" | "alc" | "ip" | "rf" selects which stacked arc the value reads on; `lit` boolean, default true; `lamp` "cool" | "amber")
- machine: the rectangular meter on the Kenwood TS-520 / TS-820 (cool green-white) and Yaesu FT-101 (amber) HF transceivers, 1970s
- era: 1970s
- origin: Japan
- size: 60 × 40 mm rectangular meter in a black panel scrap → build at 170 × 120 px
- materials: a rectangular black plastic bezel with a slightly convex smoked plastic window; a white scale card backlit from below-left so it glows unevenly (cool green-white, or amber on the Yaesu); three or four stacked arcs — "S 1 3 5 7 9 +20 +40 +60 dB" with a red band beyond S9, "ALC" with a red zone at the right, "IP 0 100 200 300 mA", "RF 0 … 10"; a black pointer with a red tip; a black panel with a fine brushed texture
- palette: bezel #141414, window smoke #000 at 10 %, card lit cool #dfeee2 with a #b9d9c2 pool at the lower left, or amber #f4d79a with a #e2b662 pool, unlit #cfcbc0, scales #171717, red bands #c8261c, pointer #111 with a #c8261c tip, panel #1a1b1c with a horizontal grain #262728
- typeface: Google "Roboto Condensed" 700 at 8 px for the S figures; "Roboto Condensed" 500 6 px for the other scales; "Roboto Condensed" 700 caps 6 px for "S", "ALC", "IP", "RF" at the left ends of each arc
- the tells:
  1. stacked arcs: four concentric scales with their labels at the left end, S at the top; the meter reads on whichever one `scale` selects (the others stay printed)
  2. the backlight is *uneven* — a pool of light lower-left where the lamp sits, fading toward the upper right, so the card is brighter near the pivot
  3. the S9+ red band and the ALC red zone are on the right, the two reds not aligned
  4. the pointer has a red tip and a black shaft, and pivots from a small chrome-capped boss at the bottom centre
  5. the window is smoked and slightly convex with a low horizontal glint; the bezel is plain black plastic with a soft moulding radius
  6. at `lit="false"` the card goes dull grey-cream and the reds darken
- motion: 150 ms rise, 400 ms fall; on `scale="alc"` the fall is faster (200 ms) and the needle twitches with speech-like bursts in `demo(t)`
- states to show: S at 60 (S9+12) cool-lit; ALC at 70 amber; one at scale 0.7 unlit
- priority: B

## F15 · Galvanometer with mirror and lamp (spot galvanometer)

### F15.1 · Pye Scalamp — grey box, milky horizontal scale, lit spot with a hairline
- slug: `galvo-pye-scalamp-spot`
- element: `sk-galvo-scalamp`
- kind: output
- value: signed range −25…+25 step 0.1 unit mm (`sensitivity` attribute "×1" | "×0.1" | "×0.01" | "CLAMP" only labels the knob; `lamp` boolean, default true)
- machine: W.G. Pye & Co. "Scalamp" moving-coil spot galvanometer with built-in lamp and scale, Cambridge, 1930s–1970s
- era: 1950s
- origin: UK
- size: 6 × 8-inch box front with the scale across the top → build at 260 × 200 px
- materials: a grey hammertone-painted steel box with rounded corners; across the top front a **horizontal milky ground-glass scale** ~180 mm long, centre-zero, with black figures every 5 and fine mm ticks; a bright light spot ~6 mm wide with a sharp vertical hairline in its middle, thrown from inside; below the scale, a black bakelite knob with a skirt marked ×1 ×0.1 ×0.01 CLAMP, two brass terminals, and an engraved black-filled panel plate with a generic "GALVANOMETER" legend
- palette: hammertone #8d9294 with a #b3b8ba mottle and #5b6062 dimples, scale glass #e9ebe6 lit from behind to #f6f7f2 in the middle, figures #1a1a18, spot #fff8d6 with a hot core #ffffff and a soft #ffe9a8 halo (blur 4 px), hairline #1a1a18, knob #1b1917 with a #3a3633 highlight, terminals brass #b99a4c, plate #dfe1dc with #1a1a18 engraving
- typeface: Gill-like → Google "Libre Franklin" 500 at 8 px for the scale figures "25 20 15 10 5 0 5 10 15 20 25"; "Libre Franklin" 600 caps 6 px tracking 0.2em for the plate and the knob skirt
- the tells:
  1. the reading is a *light spot*, not a needle: a soft bright ellipse with a crisp black vertical hairline down its middle, sliding along a milky scale; the spot is brightest at its centre and fades at its ends
  2. the scale is *horizontal* and *linear*, centre-zero, with figures every 5 that repeat on both sides and fine ticks every 1 — a ruler, not an arc
  3. the milky glass glows very faintly all along (the lamp lights it a little); a darker band at the top and bottom edges where the metal frame overlaps it
  4. grey hammertone paint with a real mottle texture (radial blobs at 3–5 px, 15 % contrast) and slightly rounded box corners with a brighter edge
  5. the sensitivity knob with its printed skirt below the scale on the left, two brass terminals on the right, and the engraved plate between
  6. the spot lags and *overshoots* on a change, swinging past and back — a light mirror on a suspension, not a pivot
  7. `lamp="false"` kills the spot and leaves the milky scale dead grey
- motion: suspension ballistics — 900 ms with a 15 % overshoot and three decaying swings (critically under-damped); when idle the spot has a 0.2 mm 0.5 Hz drift
- states to show: −8.5; +17.2; one at scale 0.6 with `sensitivity="CLAMP"` (spot parked at 0)
- priority: A

### F15.2 · Kelvin mirror galvanometer — the spot on a distant paper scale
- slug: `galvo-kelvin-mirror-cable`
- element: `sk-galvo-kelvin-scale`
- kind: output
- value: signed range −100…+100 step 1 unit mm (the scale is a metre long, centre-zero)
- machine: Thomson (Kelvin) mirror galvanometer's lamp-and-scale as used on the Atlantic telegraph, James White, Glasgow, 1858–1880s
- era: 1860s
- origin: UK
- size: a 300 × 60 mm slice of the metre scale in its wooden frame, with the slit lamp's spot → build at 320 × 90 px
- materials: a long ivory paper scale printed with figures every 10 and mm ticks, mounted on a mahogany strip with a brass edge; above it a narrow dark slit through which a warm oil-lamp light throws a fuzzy bright spot ~10 mm wide; the paper has foxing and a fold; a brass wire hairline across the slit is the reference at 0
- palette: paper #efe4c8 with foxing #c9b38c at 30 %, figures #2a2519 (engraved-look), mahogany #5c2f1a → #7a4426, brass edge #c9a24c, spot #ffd98a core #fff2c8 halo #ffb64a at 25 % (blur 6 px), slit #111, hairline #a68a3e
- typeface: engraved Victorian figures → Google "Libre Franklin" 600 at 9 px, with small caps "DIVISIONS" at the right end in "Libre Franklin" 600 caps 5 px tracking 0.3em
- the tells:
  1. a warm, fuzzy oil-lamp spot — soft-edged, yellow-orange, without a hairline — swinging along a very long paper scale that mostly runs off both ends of the element
  2. the scale is ivory paper printed with figures every 10 that read outward from 0 in both directions, with a small fold crease and foxing spots
  3. the mahogany rail and brass edge below the paper, with two brass screws
  4. the dark slit above the paper through which the spot comes, with a brass hairline wire at 0
  5. the spot swings slowly and hugely, overshooting by a third and taking seconds to settle — the Morse of a cable operator's dot and dash is the spot's left-and-right
  6. a `demo(t)` that sends a slow Morse "V" as spot deflections
- motion: very slow suspension — 2 s with a 30 % overshoot and four decaying swings; the spot's brightness flickers ±5 % at 3 Hz (an oil flame)
- states to show: +40; −65; one at scale 0.7 running the Morse demo
- priority: B

# G · Numerals and characters

*Build-ready style entries for codes G1–G17, chosen from `p2-FG.md`. One
priority-A entry per code (the definitive example), the rest B or C. Every
entry names the machine for reference only — builds use generic wordmarks
and never reproduce a logo. Google-Font stand-ins are from SPEC §3's list.
Seven-segment, Nixie, Numitron, Panaplex, VFD and LED digits are SVG paths
or CSS segments, never a font; each entry gives the segment geometry, the
glow colour and the bloom. Dot-matrix characters come from a 5×7 glyph
table in the element, not a font. Sizes are the natural size at `scale="1"`
in CSS px and include the window, bezel or panel scrap the element carries;
small objects (watch faces, tube close-ups) are built at a stated
magnification so they are legible at scale 1. Digit outputs animate their
mechanism (a drum rolls, a flap falls, a cathode cross-fades); every entry
says how. Slugs here use the prefixes `counter-`, `odometer-`,
`tape-counter-`, `flap-`, `nixie-`, `numitron-`, `panaplex-`, `vfd-`,
`led7-`, `lcd-`, `dotmatrix-`, `flipdot-`, `dekatron-`, `flag-`, `wheel-`,
`plasma-`, `print-` and `tape-` so they never collide with the F and H
`led-`, `neon-` and `bargraph-` slugs.*

## G1 · Drum counter / odometer

### G1.1 · Veeder-Root cast-case counter with knurled reset knob
- slug: `counter-veeder-root-cast`
- element: `sk-counter-veeder-root`
- kind: output
- value: digits 0–99999 (attribute `digits` sets the wheel count, default 5; `reset` attribute draws the side knob, and `resettable` makes it a click-to-zero momentary control)
- machine: Veeder-Root "Series 1200 / Little Giant" mechanical revolution counter in a cast-zinc case, Hartford CT, 1920s–1970s
- era: 1930s
- origin: USA
- size: case ~64 × 38 mm with a 40 × 11 mm window, knob standing 12 mm proud on the right → build at 176 × 100 px
- materials: dull cast-zinc case with rounded corners and a raised rim around the window; the window is a slot cut in the casting with a glass insert set back 2 px; five ivory numeral wheels with black figures, the drum edges visible as darker crescents; a knurled black-phenolic or nickel reset knob on a shaft at the right; two mounting ears with screw holes top and bottom
- palette: zinc #8e8f8a with shadow #55574f and highlight #c5c6c0, window rebate #2b2b28, ivory drums #efe6cc, drum shadow gradient to #a89f86 at the top and bottom of each cell, figures #1a1814, knob #262421 with knurl highlights #6b6862, glass reflection #ffffff at 7 %
- typeface: engraved-drum figures, a plain grotesque → Google "Roboto Condensed" 500 at 18 px, drawn as text nodes on a vertical strip that translates
- the tells:
  1. each wheel is a vertical strip of 0–9 seen through the window; the cylinder is suggested by a top/bottom darkening gradient (drum curvature) on every cell, and the figure itself is squashed 6 % at the extreme top and bottom of the window
  2. the last wheel rolls continuously — at value 1234.6 the units wheel shows 4 sliding up with 5 half-in — and each higher wheel only moves during the last 10 % of the wheel below (the carry), so a row of nines rolls together like a wave
  3. the window rim is a raised lip of the casting with a bevel highlight on the top edge and a shadow on the bottom; a thin black shadow line between the drums and the rim shows they sit inside the case
  4. a fine vertical seam line between adjacent wheels (the spacer washers), 1 px #6d6552
  5. the knurled knob on the right with ~24 knurl lines and a turned end; when `resettable` it turns 30° and springs back on click
  6. a generic cast-in wordmark ("ROOT COUNTER") in 5 px caps, slightly raised, above the window; "No. 0000" stamped small below
  7. the zinc has a faint sand-cast texture (2 px noise at 4 % opacity) and a soft matte sheen, never chrome
- motion: an increment rolls the units wheel over 180 ms ease-in-out with a 2 px overshoot and settle (the ratchet); a jump of many counts spins at up to 12 digits/s and decelerates; reset spins every wheel back to 0 at once over 400 ms
- states to show: 01234 static; a live counter incrementing once a second with the last wheel half-rolled; 00000 just after a reset click at scale 1.25
- priority: A

### G1.2 · Car odometer with the red tenths drum in a speedometer slot
- slug: `odometer-vdo-red-tenths`
- element: `sk-odometer-vdo`
- kind: output
- value: digits 0–999999.9 (six black wheels plus a tenths wheel; `trip` boolean adds a smaller four-wheel trip counter beneath with a reset stalk drawn, not interactive)
- machine: VDO / Stewart-Warner six-drum odometer as set into the speedometer face of a 1960s–70s European or American car (VW Beetle, Porsche 911, Ford Mustang)
- era: 1960s
- origin: Germany / USA
- size: slot ~36 × 6 mm in the dial → build at ×3, 216 × 44 px for the slot plus 8 px of black dial around it
- materials: a rectangular slot punched in a matte black dial with a hairline chrome or white-paint surround; six white-on-black drums plus one white-on-red tenths drum; the drums visibly cylindrical, catching a highlight at the top; a tiny "km" or "MILES" legend in the dial below
- palette: dial #141414, slot surround #d9d9d6 (1 px), drums #1c1c1c with cylinder highlight #4a4a4a at the top and shadow #050505 at the bottom, figures #f2f2ee, tenths drum #b8241e with highlight #d9433a, figures on red #fbf7f0, seam lines #333
- typeface: a narrow DIN-like drum figure → Google "Oswald" 400 at 22 px, with the figures slightly extended horizontally (scaleX 1.1) as VDO drums are
- the tells:
  1. the tenths drum is the only colour on the instrument: red with white figures, spinning continuously as the vehicle moves
  2. white figures on black drums with a visible drum curvature — a soft highlight band across the top third of each cell
  3. the drums are packed tight with 1 px dark seams, and the whole row sits 2 px back from the dial face with a shadow on its top edge (the slot has depth)
  4. the units drum moves only when the tenths completes a turn; the carry is a snap, not a roll — 60 ms
  5. the hairline surround is drawn only on the top and bottom edges of the slot, the way a painted dial has it
  6. the trip counter, when shown, is smaller (0.7 ×), white-on-black without a red drum, with a tiny knurled stalk end sticking down-right
  7. a "MILES" or "km" legend in 6 px white caps under the slot
- motion: the tenths drum rolls continuously at a rate derived from consecutive `value` sets (velocity-follow, 150 ms smoothing); higher drums carry with a 60 ms snap
- states to show: 048273.6; 099999.9 about to roll over; with `trip` at 0421 beneath
- priority: B

### G1.3 · Hengstler black DIN counter with a red last drum
- slug: `counter-hengstler-din-red`
- element: `sk-counter-hengstler`

- machine: Hengstler 0 466 / Kübler "Compact" German panel counter in a small black plastic case with a rectangular bezel, Aldingen, 1960s–90s

- palette: bezel #1b1b1b with chamfer highlight #3a3a3a, window rebate #0a0a0a, drums #202020 with highlight #3d3d3d, figures #f4f4f0, red drum #c0261e / highlight #d84a3f, lever #232323, legend white #e8e8e4

## G3 · Split-flap

### G3.1 · Solari Cifra 3 cylinder flip clock
- slug: `flap-solari-cifra-3`
- element: `sk-flap-cifra-3`
- kind: output
- value: time HH:MM (24-hour by default, `twelve` boolean shows 12-hour with a small AM/PM flap); `case` = "black" | "white" | "orange" | "red"
- machine: Solari di Udine "Cifra 3" table clock designed by Gino Valle, 1966–present; MoMA design collection
- era: 1960s
- origin: Italy
- size: cylinder 180 × 100 mm dia, window 112 × 48 mm → build at 360 × 200 px
- materials: a horizontal ABS cylinder with a flat front face where the window is; the cylinder ends are flat discs; a rectangular window with a slight lip; behind it two flap drums — hours (00–23) in one, minutes (00–59) in another — of black plastic flaps with white figures; the split line across the middle of each figure; a small ridged setting wheel at the back
- palette: black case #1a1a1a with cylinder highlight #3c3c3c along the top and shadow #050505 under; white case #f2f1ec / #d8d6ce; orange #e8591c; red #c4262b; flaps #111 with the flap edge highlight #333, figures #f7f7f4; the split line #000 at 1 px with a #2a2a2a lower edge
- typeface: Helvetica on the flaps → Google "Inter" 600 at 84 px for the figures, tracking −0.02em (white on black, the figure split horizontally across two flaps)
- the tells:
  1. the case is a cylinder seen from the front: the flat face with the window is a vertical band with a soft highlight along the top curve and a deep shadow below; the whole object reads as a tube
  2. two large flap groups, hours and minutes, each figure cut across its middle by the split line; the two halves are never quite vertically aligned (offset 0.5 px) as real flaps hang
  3. the flip: the top half of the current figure hinges down over 130 ms (3D rotateX from 0° to −90° with perspective 600 px), revealing the next figure's top half already in place; then the falling flap continues from +90° to 0° as the next figure's bottom half over 110 ms with a small bounce
  4. the falling flap is darker on its underside and casts a moving shadow on the flap below
  5. the minutes drum has two flaps per digit position — units and tens flip independently, so :09 → :10 is a two-flap cascade
  6. a small moulded bar beside the window on the right (the setting wheel access) and the model's typical thin recess line running around the front face
  7. the figures are large and geometric — Helvetica-like — with no serifs and a closed 4 (a Cifra tell)
- motion: the flip as above; when the clock is set live, flips happen on the minute
- states to show: 10:24 black case; 23:59 about to roll to 00:00 with the flap mid-fall; orange case at scale 0.7
- priority: A

- era: 1970s
- origin: Italy

- materials: a black steel frame with a slight satin sheen; each character a stack of 40 black flaps in its own module with a 1 px gap between modules; white sans letters; the module has a small black lip top and bottom hiding the flap axles

- the tells:
  1. every character is a separate module, so a row is a row of small black boxes each with its own split line, not one continuous strip
  2. the wave: when the text changes, modules start flipping left-to-right with a 40 ms stagger, each module cycling through the intermediate flaps (at ~12 flaps/s) until it reaches its target letter — so early letters settle while later ones are still fluttering

  5. a blank flap is not black-empty but shows the same split line — the module is always "displaying"
  6. an optional column-header strip above in 6 px white caps ("TIME · DESTINATION · GATE") on a dark grey band
  7. the row sits in a frame with a thin bright edge at the top only, the way overhead boards are lit from above
- motion: the wave as above; a single-character change flips only that module; a subtle 0.3 px vertical jitter on flaps while in motion
- states to show: "ZURICH HB   14:35"; mid-wave between "MILANO C.LE" and "VENEZIA S.L."; a 4-cell "GATE B12" module at scale 1.5

## G4 · Nixie tube

### G4.1 · Soviet IN-14 Nixie in a socket
- slug: `nixie-in14-socket`
- element: `sk-nixie-in14`
- kind: output
- value: digits 0–999999 (attribute `digits` sets the tube count, default 4; `colon` adds INS-1 neon colon lamps between pairs; `ghost` level 0–1, default 0.35)
- machine: Soviet ИН-14 Nixie tube (1970s–80s) in a black-phenolic socket on a dark board, as in a Ч3-34 counter or a hobby clock
- era: 1970s
- origin: USSR
- size: 19 mm dia × 43 mm tube, digit 18 mm tall → build at 48 × 96 px per tube at ×2.5, tubes on a 52 px pitch
- materials: a clear glass envelope with a rounded top and a faint blue-grey edge; inside, ten stacked thin-metal cathode digits seen edge-on as dark ghost shapes; a fine hexagonal anode mesh in front of the stack; the lit cathode glows orange with a pink-white core; a black phenolic socket with a ring of pin holes at the base; a red-black board underneath
- palette: glow core #ffd9a8, glow body #ffb26b, halo #ff6a1a at 45 % → #ff3a5a at 10 % at the outer edge, unlit cathodes #3a2d28, mesh #2a2320 at 25 %, glass edge #7f8890 at 40 % with a #ffffff 60 % highlight on the top-left, socket #1b1917, board #2b1a1a
- typeface: none — the digit shapes are the IN-14's own, drawn as SVG paths: a single stroke 2.4 px wide at ×2.5 with round caps; the 5 is a rotated 2 (the IN-14 tell); the 1 is a plain stroke; the 4 has an open top; the 0 is a tall oval
- the tells:
  1. the lit digit is a single continuous stroke that glows: a 3-layer stack — the path in glow-body colour, the same path with a 1.5 px blur in the core colour, and a 6 px blur in the halo colour underneath at 45 %, with a large 14 px blur at 10 % for the tube's overall orange cast
  2. the unlit cathodes: all nine other digits drawn behind the lit one in #3a2d28 at 0.9 px, stacked with a 0.4 px horizontal offset each so they read as a dark tangle; the ones in front of the lit digit occlude it slightly (a `ghost` multiplied darkening)
  3. the anode mesh over everything: a hexagonal SVG pattern of 3 px cells at 25 % opacity, only within the envelope's front face
  4. the envelope: a tall rounded-rectangle glass with a specular streak down the left, a fainter one on the right, and a darker top nipple (the evacuation tip)
  5. the base: a black phenolic socket with a ring of 13 pin holes and a small keyway; the tube's pins visible as dark stubs between glass and socket
  6. the 5 is an upside-down 2 — draw it as the 2 path rotated 180°; also the 3 has a flat top
  7. with `colon`, two small neon lamps (INS-1 type) between tube pairs glow the same orange with a smaller halo
- motion: a digit change cross-fades over 120 ms with the outgoing cathode fading through the ghost colour (a brief 60 ms dim orange after-image); a random 0.5–1.5 % flicker on the halo opacity at ~30 Hz to give the glow life; `demo(t)` counts seconds
- states to show: 1979; 0042 with colons; a single tube at scale 1.5 showing the 5
- priority: A

## G5 · Numitron / incandescent filament segment

### G5.1 · RCA DR2000 Numitron filament tube
- slug: `numitron-rca-dr2000`
- element: `sk-numitron-dr2000`
- kind: output
- value: digits 0–9999 (`digits` 1–6, default 4; `filter` = "none" | "red" for the Heathkit-style red window; `warm` 0–1 the filament drive level)
- machine: RCA DR2000 Numitron seven-segment incandescent readout in a 9-pin miniature (T-6½) envelope, 1970–80s
- era: 1970s
- origin: USA
- size: 19 mm dia × 45 mm tube, digit 14 mm tall → build at 44 × 90 px per tube at ×2.3, 52 px pitch
- materials: a clear glass miniature valve envelope with a rounded top; a black ceramic segment plate inside with seven tungsten filaments stretched across it, each filament slightly bowed; the filaments glow warm yellow-orange; a mica support disc at the top; a 9-pin base with a black plastic wafer
- palette: filament core #fff2c8, filament body #ffb84a, halo #ff8a20 at 35 %, cool-down #a8341c, unlit filament #4a3a30 at 60 %, segment plate #141210, glass edge #8a9296 at 40 %, highlight #fff at 55 %, base wafer #1a1816, pins #8c8c88
- typeface: none — seven segments as SVG paths: each a thin filament line 1.1 px wide with a slight sag (a quadratic curve bowed 1.5 px toward the tube centre), NOT a bar; segment length 14 px, the two verticals per side meeting the horizontals at a 1 px gap; the 7-seg layout is upright (no slant); the 6 and 9 have tails, the 7 no tail
- the tells:
  1. the segments are wires, not bars: hairline filaments with a visible sag and tiny bright end-posts where they meet the plate (2 px dots in #d9d2c0)
  2. incandescent colour — a warm yellow-white core with an orange halo, unlike the pink-orange of neon; a soft 5 px bloom only, no wide cast
  3. warm-up and cool-down: a segment coming on ramps from dull red #a8341c through orange to yellow-white over ~180 ms; going off it decays through orange-red over ~350 ms (the after-glow)
  4. the unlit filaments are visible as faint dark-grey wires on the black segment plate — the whole figure-8 scaffold is always there
  5. the envelope is a miniature valve: a domed top with an evacuation tip, a mica disc, and a black base wafer with the pin circle; the glass has a tall specular streak
  6. with `filter="red"`, a translucent red rectangle (#b0100a at 55 %) covers the tubes; the filaments then read as orange-red and the plate disappears
  7. at `warm` below 1 the filaments dim to orange — a real Numitron on low drive
- motion: the ramp/decay timing above per segment; `demo(t)` counts up slowly so the decays overlap
- states to show: 0982; 1234 behind a red filter; one tube at scale 1.5 mid-change from 3 to 4 with the decaying segments visible
- priority: A

- palette: phosphor lit #7dffd6 body, core #d6fff2, bloom #38e6b8 at 35 % radius 4 px, through the smoke the body reads #6ee8c4; unlit segments #14211e at 50 % (barely visible ghost); window glass #0d1110 with a 5 % #8c9a96 reflection streak; bezel #161616; chrome line #cfd2d0; legend lit #8dffe0

  5. a small segmented level bar at the right: eight short phosphor bars, the top one via a filter drawn in amber #ffc46a (the peak) — a tell of the era
  6. the seconds tick with a 60 ms fade, and on a track change the number blanks for 100 ms then relights
  7. the smoked window has a darker bezel edge and a single diagonal reflection band

- era: 1990s

- materials: a reflective TN LCD with a grey-green field; black segments with a faint shadow offset (the polariser doubling); a pale ghost of every unlit segment; a tiny printed frame around the display with the mode legends in white and the "ALARM" / "SIGNAL" pictogram row; a black resin bezel with radiused corners and a small "WR" style generic legend
- palette: field #a8b39c (grey-green), field under LIGHT #b8b070, lit segment #1c1e1a, segment shadow #1c1e1a at 18 % offset 0.6 px down-right, unlit ghost #93a08a at 35 %, frame #dbe0d4 printed line, bezel #1a1a1a with #333 highlight, legend white #e6e8e2, accent cyan #2ab5c8 for a printed line (generic, no logo)

- the tells:
  1. slanted black segments on a grey-green reflective field, with every unlit segment visible as a pale ghost — the LCD's most characteristic quality
  2. the doubled shadow: each lit segment has a faint offset copy (the polariser gap), so the digits look very slightly embossed
  3. the layout: small day + date top-left, big HH:MM, smaller seconds at the right, "PM" tiny at the left, alarm and signal pictograms along the top under a thin printed line
  4. the field is not uniform: a soft diagonal gradient of reflected light (2 % lighter at upper-left) and the segments disappear at extreme viewing (not simulated, but the ghost is)
  5. the LIGHT state tints the field to an amber-green from the lower-left corner (the single micro-lamp)
  6. the bezel legends "LIGHT · ALARM · MODE" at the corners, small, white; a thin cyan printed line above the display
  7. the seconds tick with no fade — LCD segments switch in a hard 30 ms, but with a barely visible 15 % "bleed" ghost for 100 ms after switching off (slow LCD)
- motion: as above; stopwatch mode runs at 1/100 s; the demo cycles modes

- era: 1980s
- origin: USA

## G11 · Flip-dot / flip-disc

### G11.1 · Ferranti-Packard yellow flip-disc matrix module
- slug: `flipdot-ferranti-packard-matrix`
- element: `sk-flipdot-ferranti-packard`
- kind: output
- value: bits — a `columns` × `rows` bitmap (default 28 × 7), or `text` rendered from the element's 5×7 table; `disc` px (default 14)
- machine: Ferranti-Packard flip-disc (Kenyon Taylor, Toronto) as installed on the Montreal Stock Exchange board (1961), airport gate signs and transit boards, 1961–1990s
- era: 1960s
- origin: Canada
- size: 10 mm discs on a 12 mm pitch, a 28 × 7 module ~ 340 × 90 mm → build at 14 px pitch, 392 × 98 px plus an 8 px black frame
- materials: a matte black steel panel with a round hole per disc; each disc a fluorescent yellow-green painted aluminium disc on a pivot, the reverse black; a tiny pivot pin visible at the disc's edge; the panel between discs is dead black; a frame with screw heads
- palette: disc yellow #d6e600 with a lighter #eaf53a edge and a #9fae00 lower shadow, disc black side #141414 with a #2a2a2a rim, panel #0c0c0c, hole rim #1f1f1f, pivot pin #8a8a86, frame #1a1a1a
- typeface: none — a 5×7 glyph table; the element also accepts a raw bitmap
- the tells:
  1. round yellow-green discs on black — the discs are slightly smaller than their holes so a dark ring surrounds each, and a tiny pivot pin shows at the 3 o'clock edge of every disc
  2. the flip: a disc turning on rotates about its vertical pivot over 60 ms (scaleX 1 → 0 → 1 with the colour swapping at the midpoint), so a changing character shows a flicker of thin edge-on discs
  3. the discs never all move at once: an update sweeps across the module column by column at ~6 columns per frame, giving a visible ripple
  4. the yellow is a matte fluorescent paint with no specular; the black side has a faint rim highlight
  5. one or two discs per module are randomly "sticky" (seeded): they flip 80 ms late — the tell of a real board
  6. the panel is matte black with a fine 2 % noise; the frame has four screw heads and a dark gap between adjacent modules
  7. an optional `backlight` boolean lights the discs from behind-fluorescent as on airport boards, brightening the yellow to #f0ff40
- motion: as above; the demo cycles stock-style rows ("XYZ 42 1/2 +1/4")
- states to show: "GATE 12"; a bitmap arrow; a sweep mid-update at scale 1.2
- priority: A

## G12 · Dekatron / counting tube

### G12.1 · Ericsson GS10C Dekatron end view — the stepping orange dot
- slug: `dekatron-ericsson-gs10c`
- element: `sk-dekatron-gs10c`
- kind: output
- value: steps 0–9 (the glow position; `value` is the count modulo 10) with a `delta` input mode that accepts pulses via `step()`; `glow` = "orange" | "purple" (the Soviet ОГ-4 tint); `demo(t)` spins at a slowly varying rate
- machine: Ericsson Telephones GS10C / GC10B decade counting tube, Beeston, 1949–60s; the Harwell Dekatron computer's readout
- era: 1950s
- origin: UK
- size: 1″ dia tube seen end-on → build at ×3.5, 96 × 96 px plus a 12 px black holder ring
- materials: a round glass end-face with a domed top; inside, a central disc anode and a ring of 30 fine wire cathodes (10 main, 20 guide) standing up from a mica disc; one main cathode glows with an orange neon dot; a black bakelite holder ring with a slot; the glass edge with a bright ring highlight
- palette: glow core #ffd7a0, glow body #ff8a30, halo #ff4a1a at 45 % radius 6 px, guide-cathode faint glow #ff6a2a at 12 %, cathode wires #7a7068, anode disc #2c2a26 with #4a4640 highlight, mica #b8b0a0 at 40 %, glass edge #9aa4a8 at 45 %, dome highlight #fff at 50 %, holder #1a1816
- typeface: none; an optional printed 0–9 escutcheon ring around the holder in Google "Libre Franklin" 500 at 7 px
- the tells:
  1. a ring of 30 tiny cathode pins seen end-on as short radial dashes around a dark central disc — 10 slightly longer main ones and 20 shorter guides between
  2. one orange dot glowing on a main cathode with a small halo; when stepping, the glow visibly hops via the two guide cathodes (three 8 ms sub-steps: main → guide 1 → guide 2 → next main) so a fast count reads as a rotating smear
  3. the dome: a big round glass face with a bright crescent highlight at the upper-left and a darker rim ring, inside a black holder with a keyway slot
  4. the central anode disc is a dull grey with a slight radial brush; the mica sheet behind the ring is faintly visible
  5. reverse counting (negative `delta`) hops the other way — the glow can go anti-clockwise
